**The Whisper of Forgotten Things**

There’s a quiet magic in the things we leave behind—the half-finished books on dusty shelves, the single sock that vanished in the laundry, the coffee cup left on a train seat, still warm when the next passenger sits down. These are the ghosts of our daily lives, the silent witnesses to moments we’ve already forgotten.

I think about the woman who once lived in my apartment before me. Sometimes, when I’m scrubbing the bathroom tiles, I wonder if her hands touched the same grout, if she cursed the same stubborn stain. Did she, too, stand at this window and watch the rain blur the streetlights into halos? The walls remember, even if we don’t.

We’re all just temporary custodians of spaces and objects. The pen you lose will write someone else’s grocery list. The shirt you donate will hug a stranger’s shoulders. The house you sell will echo with new laughter, new arguments, new silence. It’s humbling, in a way—this constant passing of things from hand to hand, life to life.

And yet, we cling. We hoard journals we’ll never reread, keep clothes that no longer fit, save ticket stubs from concerts we barely remember. Maybe it’s fear—that if we let go of the physical, the memories will dissolve like sugar in tea. But memories aren’t in things; they’re in the way the light slanted through the blinds at 3 PM on a Tuesday, in the scent of rain on hot pavement that takes you back to a childhood summer. Things are just anchors. The real magic is in the drifting.

Tonight, I found a coin on the sidewalk—heads up, as if placed there just for me. I picked it up, turned it over in my fingers, and wondered whose pocket it fell from. Did they notice it was gone? Do they miss it? Or did they walk away, lighter by a single cent, unaware?

I put it in my own pocket. A tiny, metallic baton passed in the relay of the unseen.
